**Swift finds domestic delays consume 80% of cross-border payment journey times**

*New data shifts attention from interbank messaging speed to domestic processing bottlenecks, with implications for Europe's instant payments infrastructure and the G20's 2027 target.*

Swift has published its latest Spotlight on Speed report, revealing that half of cross-border payments on its network reach recipient banks within 40 seconds and 75% arrive within 10 minutes. The interbank leg of the journey is now ahead of the G20's target for one-hour end-to-end processing by 2027. But the report makes clear that speed gains in cross-border messaging are being undermined by what happens next: the last mile, from receiving institution to beneficiary account, accounts for around 80% of total processing time. In a third of the 40 receiving markets analysed, median last-mile processing sits at around one hour.

Thierry Chilosi, Swift's chief business officer, said the challenge now is to "tackle the inconsistency that we see in the last mile in markets around the world". Swift's retail payments framework, launched in June with more than 100 banks, has demonstrated end-to-end processing in seconds on some corridors, including Turkey to Spain in 15 seconds and Australia to India in 37 seconds. These routes use one-leg-out arrangements that connect international transfers directly into domestic instant payment systems.

The findings carry practical weight for European banks and payment providers. Europe's investment in instant payments infrastructure through TIPS and the instant payments regulation was designed in part to eliminate precisely these domestic delays. The report suggests that markets which have not modernised their domestic crediting processes risk becoming bottlenecks in an otherwise fast cross-border system, regardless of how quickly interbank messaging operates.

**Google's Gemini connects to bank accounts via Plaid integration**

*The integration gives Gemini read access to external bank and card accounts through open banking rails, extending AI assistants deeper into personal financial data.*

Google has connected its Gemini AI assistant to external bank accounts and payment cards through an integration with Plaid, alongside native access to Google Wallet data. Users can link accounts from outside the Google ecosystem, with Plaid providing masked account access without exposing bank passwords.

OpenAI's ChatGPT connected to bank accounts earlier this year, and Gemini's integration extends the broader race among AI platform operators to embed financial data into their assistants. For European open banking providers and banks, each new AI platform that gains read access to account data raises questions about consent management, data minimisation and the adequacy of existing API frameworks to govern non-traditional third-party access.

Gemini's integration currently appears to offer read-only access rather than payment initiation. But the direction of travel is clear: AI assistants are positioning themselves as the interface layer between consumers and their financial lives, a dynamic that open banking regulators and incumbents will need to account for as open finance frameworks mature.

stories.original:
**Bank of England confirms industry support for UK retail payments redesign**

*A total of 121 consultation responses back the core design direction set out earlier this year, moving the Retail Payments Infrastructure Board closer to its next phase.*

Victoria Cleland, the Bank of England's executive director for payments, has confirmed that all 121 responses to the central bank's consultation supported the proposed design direction for the UK's next-generation retail payments infrastructure. The consultation, which followed the Retail Payments Infrastructure Board's (RPIB) design paper published in the summer, asked whether the outlined approach struck the right balance between modernisation and continuity.

The RPIB, which includes industry participants alongside the UK's Financial Conduct Authority and Payment Systems Regulator as observers, is now expected to move into more detailed specification work. The breadth of support removes a significant procedural hurdle, though the harder questions around technical architecture, migration timelines and funding remain ahead.

The confirmation comes as the UK government consults separately on modernising payments regulation more broadly, including the future roles of Pay.UK and the PSR. The two workstreams are running in parallel but will need to converge: the regulatory framework under which a new infrastructure operates matters as much as its design.

stories.original:
**Planky raises €6.9m to build AI credit decisioning on open banking data**

*A pivot from open banking analytics toward real-time AI-powered lending decisions reflects broader market convergence between open banking data access and automated credit infrastructure.*

Planky is raising €6.9 million to transform its open banking analytics platform into a real-time AI credit decisioning layer for lenders and digital platforms. The funding positions the company at the intersection of two trends reshaping European lending: cashflow-based underwriting using open banking data and AI-driven automation of credit decisions.

The raise sits alongside a string of similar moves in recent months. Experian launched a consumer reporting agency for cashflow-based underwriting in October, Plaid released AI models for lending decisions the same month, and PayPoint completed its acquisition of open banking credit data firm AperiData in June. The pattern suggests open banking's role in lending is shifting from supplementary data source to primary decisioning input.

For banks and payment providers, the competitive implication is that the infrastructure connecting account data to credit decisions is becoming a distinct product category. Firms that treat open banking APIs as compliance obligations rather than commercial assets risk ceding the credit decisioning layer to specialist intermediaries.
